chunks.text:
#### What do I do if my clothes catch on fire?

If you are on fire, use STOP, DROP, and ROLL:

1. Stop what you are doing.
2. Drop to the ground and cover your face if you can.
3. Roll over and over or back and forth until the flames go out. Running while on fire will only make the fire burn faster.

#### What are the first things I should do when I see a fire?

1. SOUND THE ALARM — Call 911 and pull any fire alarm immediately if you see an uncontrolled fire.
2. GET OUT OF THE DANGER ZONE — Evacuate yourself and those around you out of the building. Get away from the fire until you are no longer feeling the heat (further is better in case something explodes). Close the doors behind you. DO NOT USE ELEVATORS.

AVOID breathing, touching, or running through fire. Get low to the ground to avoid breathing in smoke as you evacuate. If possible, cover your mouth with a damp cloth to help you breathe.
chunks.sectionPath: During (React) > If You Are Near a Fire:

chunks.text:
#### When is a fire too large for one person to put out?

NEVER attempt to fight a large fire. If you are uncomfortable attempting to put out the blaze or the flames are taller than you or cover an area larger than 60 square feet (about the size of a king bed) it is too large for a person alone to extinguish.
chunks.sectionPath: During (React) > If You Are Near a Fire:

chunks.text:
#### What should I do if a small fire starts on the stovetop?

If the fire just started and is small:
1. Put a lid over the flames or use a fire extinguisher.
2. Leave the pan covered until it is completely cooled.

If you try to fight the fire, be sure others are getting out and you have a clear way out. If the fire is large: evacuate, close the door behind you to help contain the fire, and call 9-1-1 after you leave.
chunks.sectionPath: During (React) > If You Are Near a Fire:

chunks.text:
#### What do I do if there is a fire inside my oven?

For an oven fire: Turn off the heat and keep the door closed.
chunks.sectionPath: During (React) > If You Are Near a Fire:

chunks.text:
#### What should I yell and do if a fire breaks out at home?

Yell "Fire!" several times and go outside right away.
- Leave your things where they are and save yourself.
- Use the stairs if you live in a building with elevators.
- DO NOT OPEN HOT DOORS. Never open doors that are warm to the touch. If closed doors or handles are warm or smoke blocks your escape route, find another way out.
- Get low and go under the smoke if you must escape through the smoke to your exit. Close doors behind you.
chunks.sectionPath: During (React) > CALL 9-1-1 or your local emergency phone number.

chunks.text:
#### What should I do if smoke or fire blocks my way out of a room?

If smoke, heat, or flames block your exit routes:
- Stay in the room with doors closed.
- Place a wet towel under the door and call the fire department or 9-1-1.
- Open a window and wave a brightly colored cloth or flashlight to signal for help.
chunks.sectionPath: During (React) > CALL 9-1-1 or your local emergency phone number.

chunks.text:
#### How far away from the building should I stay once I'm out?

STAY OUTSIDE.
- Get at least 50 feet (16 meters) away from the building.
- Go to your meeting place and make sure someone has called the fire department.
- If you cannot get to your meeting place, follow your household emergency plan.

#### What should I do if my car catches fire while I'm driving?

1. Stop the car. Pull over as far off the road as safely possible.
2. Turn the ignition and battery OFF. You want to turn OFF any source that may feed the fire.
3. Get out of the car. Evacuate all occupants and step as far away as you can. Get out, stay out and do not reach for valuables. Car fires are volatile and can cause explosions or blow tires.
4. Call 911. Even if the car appears to no longer smoke or burn, get help.
5. Keep bystanders away from the car. Do not allow anyone close so no one gets hurt. If you see dry brush around, try to get it away so the woods do not ignite and cause a brushfire.

#### Why are overloaded power strips a fire hazard during holidays?

NEVER plug electrical appliances into the power strip to fill it. Every power strip has a load capacity, which means it can only move so much power through its circuits at any given time. Overloading the strip can create a fire hazard, melting the plastic and damaging your home or business as well as any surrounding equipment.

#### What do I do if my Christmas tree catches fire?

1. Cut the power, if it is safe. If the fire just began and you can safely reach the outlet where lights are plugged in, unplug the lights OR shut the power off entirely.
2. Extinguish the fire. If you have a home fire extinguisher and the fire is contained to the tree, use it (Pull the pin. Aim the nozzle. Squeeze the handle. Sweep at the bulk of the fire.)

Once the fire is out: Open windows to air out smoke until the home is clear. If the fire was not extinguished easily, call 911 right away. If you can reach the electrical breaker, shut down the power.
chunks.sectionPath: During (React) > If a holiday decoration, like a Christmas tree, is on fire:

chunks.text:
#### How should I lead children out during a fire evacuation?

Follow your area's fire evacuation procedures unless it is unsafe to do so.

Standard Evacuation Procedures:
- Once the fire alarm sounds, go to the nearest stairwell or exit.
- Do not use elevators.
- Do everything you would do in a fire drill.

#### What does the A.C.E.S. acronym mean if I'm trapped in fire or smoke?

ALERT. CONFINE. EVACUATE. SPECIAL ASSISTANCE.

Alert: Activate the fire alarm, call campus police if you have them. Assess the specific location for smoke or flame.
Confine: Stop the spread of smoke or flame by closing doors and windows.
Evacuate: Leave immediately. Do not allow anyone to go back into the building. Report you are safely out to your supervisor.
Special Assistance: Anyone that is physically unable to leave the building should stay put in the areas of refuge, which are typically stairwell landings.
chunks.sectionPath: During (React) > If you are trapped in a fire or smoke, use the acronym A.C.E.S.:

chunks.text:
#### What should adults remind kids about during a fire drill or real fire?

Remind kids to:
1. Leave belongings behind.
2. Form a single file line.
3. Remain calm and follow the adult's instructions.

Adults and guardians in charge should:
1. Retrieve the evacuation roster, like an attendance sheet and an assembly card.
2. Guide students to evacuation refuge areas as identified on Fire Drill Posters.
3. Be aware and listen for additional directions.
4. Keep a list of kids.
5. Report all injuries and missing students to responders.
chunks.sectionPath: During (React) > If you are trapped in a fire or smoke, use the acronym A.C.E.S.:

chunks.text:
#### What do I do if my pet is on fire?

1. Extinguish the fire. Splash water on them or smother the fire by patting them with a towel or blanket.
2. Rinse the burn with clean, cool water and get them to a veterinarian as soon as possible for burn treatment.

#### How do I evacuate pets from a burning building?

- Evacuate all pets outside.
- If you have more than one small pet, you can use a large pillowcase to catch them. As you catch your pets, put them inside the pillowcase. You can tie the top of the pillowcase to keep your pets inside until you are in a safe place.
- Do not use any large pet crates that will not easily fit through doors.
- Smoke inhalation can damage your pet's nose and lungs. Take them to a veterinarian as soon as possible for a full exam and care.

Frightened pets often act differently. They may bite, scratch, or hide. If needed, grab your pet by the scruff of the neck to pick them up. You can also throw a blanket over them and scoop them up wrapped inside it.

#### How do I get farm animals out safely if the barn is on fire?

Immediately call 911 if available in your area. Keep access roads open for emergency vehicles.

1. Get animals out of danger — Open barn stalls and release or lead animals to the designated safety pen. Use leads on any animals who cannot or will not run to the safe area on their own.

HORSES: Place a halter and lead on each horse as they leave their stall, if possible. Blindfold them only if necessary. Do not release horses into an area where they can easily run back to the fire — horses will run back into burning barns out of fear and confusion.

2. Once animals are evacuated — Shut off the building's electricity but only if it is safe to do so. Use the fire hose, bucket, and fire extinguishers to fight the fire. Do not attempt to fight the fire if you do not know how to safely use the equipment. As soon as possible, have each animal checked for injuries by a veterinarian. Horses who are stressed may be colic.

#### What are the four elements that create fire?

Four elements need to be present to create or sustain fire: oxygen, heat, fuel/material, and a chemical reaction. To stop a fire, you must remove one of these elements — by cooling the fire (removing heat), smothering it (removing oxygen), removing the source of the fire (removing fuel), or interrupting the chemical reaction (displacing the elements).

#### What do the fire extinguisher class letters (A, B, C, D, K) mean?

Letter classifications identify the type of fire an extinguisher can put out:

Class A — Ordinary Combustibles (wood, cloth, paper)
Class B — Flammable Liquids, Gases, Greases (gasoline, oil, paint, solvents, etc.)
Class C — Energized Electrical Equipment (anything powered by electricity from outlet or battery)
Class D — Combustible Metals (Magnesium, Aluminum, etc.)
Class K — Cooking Oils, Animal Fats, Vegetable Oil.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > Different Fire Fuels Need Specific Fire Extinguishers

chunks.text:
#### Where should I store a home fire extinguisher and how do I check it?

Keep your home fire extinguisher away from the kitchen and power strips, store it within your reach. The majority of fires occur in kitchen areas and overloaded power strips. If your fire extinguisher is in the kitchen, you will be unable to reach it in order to use it.

Typical fire extinguishers for homes can put out Class ABC fires. Once a year, check the gauge for the arrow to be in the green. If it is not in the green, either purchase a new one, have it serviced by a fire protection company, or drop by your local fire station.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > Different Fire Fuels Need Specific Fire Extinguishers

chunks.text:
#### How do I use a fire extinguisher (PASS technique)?

To operate a fire extinguisher, remember the acronym P.A.S.S.:

Pull the pin. Hold the extinguisher with the nozzle pointing away from you, and release the locking mechanism.
Aim low. Point the extinguisher at the base of the fire.
Squeeze the lever slowly and evenly.
Sweep the nozzle from side-to-side.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > Different Fire Fuels Need Specific Fire Extinguishers

chunks.text:
#### How should my household prepare for a fire emergency?

- Make sure everyone knows how to call 911 and what information the dispatcher will need.
- Confirm household members know to STOP, DROP, and ROLL if their clothes catch on fire.
- Confirm household members know how to use a fire extinguisher (PASS) and where you store it.
- Ensure that all household members know two ways to escape from every room of your home and know the family meeting spot outside.
- Establish a family emergency communications plan and ensure all household members know who to contact if they cannot find one another.
- Practice escaping from your home at least twice a year. Press the smoke alarm test button or yell "Fire" to alert everyone that they must get out.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > Different Fire Fuels Need Specific Fire Extinguishers

chunks.text:
#### Where should I install smoke alarms and how often should I test them?

DO:
- Install the right number of smoke alarms, professionals suggest a minimum one on every level of the home, outside each sleeping area, and in bedrooms.
- Test once a month and replace the batteries at least once a year.
- Change batteries at least once a year. Typically they require 9 Volt batteries. When batteries get low, the alarm beeps loudly until you change them.

DO NOT:
- NEVER disconnect the detector to stop the beeping noise! You will have no way of detecting fire in your home.
- Do not install smoke alarms near windows, doors, or ducts where drafts might interfere with their operation.
- Never paint smoke alarms. Paint, stickers, or other decorations could keep the alarms from working.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > Different Fire Fuels Need Specific Fire Extinguishers

chunks.text:
#### How do I burn candles safely?

If you are using an open-flame candle:
- Only use candles if you have a way to put out a fire quickly.
- Only burn candles when you are in the room or there is another trusted person supervising while you are out.
- Use sturdy candle holders that will not tip over or burn.
- Keep candles at least 12 inches from anything that can burn.
- Trim the wick of the candle to one-quarter inch each time the candle is lit to prevent a larger flame.

Consider using battery-operated flameless candles as a safer alternative if children, pets, or many people will be in the room; anyone with asthma or breathing problems will be in the room; or elders or persons with limited mobility will be left alone in the room with the candle.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > Different Fire Fuels Need Specific Fire Extinguishers

chunks.text:
#### What is the number one cause of home fires?

Cooking fires are the number one cause of home fires. Be on alert! If you are sleepy or have consumed alcohol, avoid the stove or stovetop.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > Different Fire Fuels Need Specific Fire Extinguishers

chunks.text:
#### How do I cook safely to prevent a kitchen fire?

- Do not leave food frying on the stovetop, grilling, boiling, or broiling food unattended.
- If you are simmering, baking, or roasting food, check it regularly, remain in the kitchen while food is cooking, and use a timer to remind you that you are cooking.
- Keep anything that can catch fire — oven mitts, wooden utensils, food packaging, towels or curtains — away from your stovetop.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > Always Stay Present With Cooking Food

chunks.text:
#### Why is smoking oil a danger sign, and what should I do if it catches fire?

Smoke is a danger sign that the oil is too hot. Keep an eye on what you fry — if you see wisps of smoke or notice the oil smells, immediately turn off the burner and/or carefully remove the pan from the burner. Heat the oil slowly to the temperature you need for frying or sautéing. Add food gently to the pot or pan so the oil does not splatter.

Always cook with a lid beside your pan. If you have a fire, slide the lid over the pan and turn off the burner. Do not remove the cover because the fire could start again. Let the pan cool for a long time. Never throw water on the fire. If the fire does not go out or you do not feel comfortable sliding a lid over the pan, get everyone out of your home and call the fire department from outside.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > Always Stay Present With Cooking Food

chunks.text:
#### What causes most electrical fires at home?

Most common causes of electrical fires:
- Faulty electrical plugs (old or broken)
- Outdated appliances
- Broken switches and receptacles
- Frayed power cords
- Poorly maintained panels and wiring

If the fire is isolated to the appliance, it will go out if the appliance power gets turned off. If the fire has ignited items around it, turning the power off may be inaccessible and dangerous.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > Always Stay Present With Cooking Food

chunks.text:
#### How can I prevent electrical fires in my home?

- Replace broken or old appliances.
- Keep up with fire, building, and safety codes by not allowing unlicensed handymen to work on your property.
- Keeping your electrical panel and circuit breakers up-to-date reduces the failure rate. If you have to reset your circuit breakers when using multiple appliances at once, contact a professional electrician.
- Be careful about the electrical demands of new smart technology, and solar batteries.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > Always Stay Present With Cooking Food

chunks.text:
#### How should I plug in and use household appliances safely?

- Replace outlets if plugs do not fit snugly or if the outlet does not accept plugs with one blade larger than the other.
- Avoid using extension cords.
- Check your electrical appliances often.
- Major appliances (refrigerators, stoves, washers, dryers, etc.) should be plugged directly into a wall outlet.

Heating Appliances:
- Heating equipment can cause fires if not used correctly.
- Choose a space heater that has an automatic shut-off in case it is tipped over.
- Place space heaters on a level surface, but not on cabinets, tables or other furniture.

Keep Grills and Burning Appliances Outside:
- Never use an oven, stovetop or grill to heat your home.
- Store propane and other heating fuels outside of your home.
- Make sure all fuel-burning equipment is safely vented to the outside to avoid carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning.

#### How should my workplace prepare for fire emergencies?

- Keep all emergency numbers handy.
- Do not overload outlets and circuits.
- Ensure proper storage of flammable materials. If your workplace handles flammable materials, they may need storage in a cabinet. Certain chemicals cannot be stored by each other or they may combust.
- Pay attention to fire-prone areas. Common fire-prone areas include: the employee break room or kitchen, large electrical storage rooms, and laboratories or other designated areas containing hazardous or flammable materials.
- Pair your inspection, testing, and maintenance program with documentation and dates of testing.

#### What should an evacuation plan at work cover?

- Note the exits and the closest one to your location.
- Exit routes must be free from barriers.
- Choose a spot away from the building where evacuating employees can gather.
- Choose someone to direct people to that location and take an accurate count once all are out.

#### What fire safety questions should I ask my employer?

- Do we have an emergency action plan?
- Where are the alarm systems located?
- When was the last emergency training?
- Where and how are hazardous materials stored?

You have a right to a safe work environment and a right to report any health and safety concerns not being addressed by your employer. If you do not feel safe in your work environment, you can file an anonymous complaint with the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration to request a safety inspection.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > Questions to ask your employer about fire safety:

chunks.text:
#### What essential items should I have ready for a fire emergency?

Most important items:
- Well-maintained smoke detectors
- A fire extinguisher
- A phone to call for help
- First aid kit with wound supplies

Other helpful items:
- Other face covering (scarf, bandanna, or clean cloth)
- Clean towels
- Fireproof safe for important documents
- A digital copy of important documents
- Bucket
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > Questions to ask your employer about fire safety:

chunks.text:
#### What should I teach kids about fire safety?

- Explain that fire is dangerous and should not be played with.
- Show kids how to dial 911 and what to tell the dispatcher if an adult is not there.
- Teach them how to STOP, DROP and ROLL if their clothes catch on fire.
- Teach them to stay close to the ground when smoke is in the air.
- Teach your children what smoke alarms sound like and what to do when they hear one.
- Show them two ways to escape from every room of your home.

#### How do I teach kids to check a door for fire before opening it?

- Teach them to check for heat or smoke before opening doors.
- If they see smoke coming around the door, do not open the door. If there is a window, stay close to it and wait for the fire department.
- If they do not see smoke, teach them to check the door for heat with the back of their hand, so they don't burn their hand on the doorknob.
- If the door is not hot and there is no smoke, they can open it, but only escape if they can see where they're going. If they cannot see their path, go back, close the door and wait for firefighters.
- Make sure to close all doors behind them — this action is life-saving.

#### Why should kids stay low when there's smoke in the house?

If you can see smoke in the house, stay as low as you can to the ground as you make your way to the exit. Heat and smoke rise. In a fire, hot smoke hurts more people than the actual flames. Teach kids they would inhale less smoke if they stay close to the ground.

#### How can I prevent common burns and scalds in young children?

- Keep kids 3 feet away while cooking, ironing or using hot appliances like space heaters, toasters, oven, etc. Teach children touching these items will hurt and burn them.
- Keep smoking materials locked up in a high place. Never leave cigarette lighters or matches where children can reach them.
- Never play with lighters or matches when you are with your children. Children may try to do the same things they see you do.
- Never hold a child when preparing or consuming hot foods or drinks. Hot food and drinks are the leading cause of burns and scalds.
- Never have running water unattended around children.
- When bathing a child, always make sure you check to make sure the water is warm.
- Turning taps off tightly prevents kids from turning them back on.
- Install small guards around fireplaces and heaters.

#### How should schools prepare to prevent and respond to fires?

Prevent fires:
- Keep paper and artwork on walls to a minimum. It may add to the fire load as well as fall on top of people trying to evacuate.
- NEVER hang artwork over electrical breaker panels!
- Add safeguards to prevent intentional fires by keeping the building well-lit.
- Have rules for storage of chemicals and flammable materials.
- Have special guidance in place for chemistry labs.
- Keep fire safety equipment on site and accessible.
- Keep current on your fire safety inspections.

Prepare for safe evacuation:
- Ensure all exits and stairways are clear.
- Ensure Fire Alarms, Smoke Detectors, Fire Extinguishers and Fire PULL Stations are operational.
- Conduct regular fire drills.
- Invite the local Fire Department to public education events.
- Have an evacuation plan posted in plain view.
- Have a special evacuation plan in place for large gatherings such as dances and assemblies.

#### How can I keep pets from starting or being caught in a fire?

- Never leave your pet alone around open flames. This includes candles, fireplaces, grills, and stoves.
- Use flameless candles to prevent a fire if the candle is knocked over. Pets, especially cats, can catch on fire by bumping into or jumping over candles.
- Fireproof your home by covering or removing stove knobs and by hiding wires that animals might chew.
- Keep young pets away from fire hazards using baby gates or crates.
- Remove tripping hazards like multiple power cords in a pile. Your pet may trip over power cords or get tangled up, pulling them halfway out and causing an electrical fire.

#### How do I include my pets in a fire escape plan?

- Include pets in your escape route plan and practice fire drills.
- Keep a collar, leash, or crate near a fire exit. Have an emergency supply bag ready with your pet's items like food, treats, a blanket, bowls, and a toy. Include a copy of your pet's medical records and any medication your pet needs.
- If you have more than one small pet, you can use a large pillowcase to catch them.
- Train your pet to come when called using their favorite treat as a reward.
- Train your pet to go to an exit door if they hear the fire alarm.
- Consider microchipping your pet.
- Make a note of where your pets like to sleep so you can find them quickly if you have to evacuate.
- Let firefighters know you have an animal in your home by putting pet alert stickers on your windows and/or doors.
- When you are not home, confine your pets so that they are close to an exit door.

#### How can I prevent fires on a farm?

- Store flammable materials away from your animals. These include hay, straw, grain dust, paint, fertilizer, blankets, and pesticides.
- Check storage temperatures. If the temperature of a pile reaches 150 degrees, spread the pile out. If the temperature reaches 175 degrees, call the fire department immediately and start moving the material out of the building.
- Store chemicals in the right containers and clearly mark each container with what is in it.
- Be aware of things that can start fires: cigarettes, machinery, motors, heaters, electric fences, broken glass, and batteries.
- Have smoke detectors and fire extinguishers in all buildings. Check them regularly and connect them to loud sirens on the outside of the building.
- Put a fire hose and buckets where they are easy to reach. Do not use them for any other purpose.
- Know how to shut off electricity in each building.

#### How should I prepare barns and pens to allow safe evacuation of animals?

- Keep easy access to the barn and pens. Have an access road that is at least 20 feet wide so that fire trucks can get to the building. The gate should also be wide enough for emergency vehicles. Do not block the road or any building doors. Keep trees and bushes trimmed back.
- Make sure your address is visible from the road. Post emergency contact lists in each building.
- Plan an evacuation route for each stall and room. Hang leads nearby. Pre-assign which pens to use during an evacuation.
- Familiarize the animals with your evacuation plans. Try to desensitize them to loud sirens and flashing lights so that they will be easier to handle during an emergency.
- Host an open house for emergency personnel so that they are familiar with your property and animals.

#### How do I prepare a chicken coop to avoid fires?

- Insulate the coop against drafts so you do not need to use heat bulbs.
- Remove cobwebs and dust along the ceiling, light bulbs, and power outlets.
- Avoid using power strips or surge protectors inside the coop. Overloaded outlets can catch fire.
- Use heavy-duty extension cords made to be used outdoors. Disconnect cords that feel hot and remove them from the coop.

#### How should I prepare for a fire if I have a disability?

Create a support network of trusted people that can help you in case of a fire:
- Inform them of where you keep your fire and medical supplies.
- You may consider giving a trusted member a key to your house or apartment.
- Contact your local fire department's non-emergency helpline and explain your needs. They can suggest escape plan ideas and may perform a home fire safety inspection.
- Ask your local dispatch to keep your special needs information on file so it is accessible to emergency responders.

Plan your escape around your capabilities:
- If you use a service animal, practice your fire escape plan with them.
- Know at least two exits from every room.
- If you use a walker or wheelchair, check all exits to be sure you can get through the doorways.

#### What smoke alarm options exist for people who are deaf or hard of hearing?

Hard-of-Hearing, Deaf Accessible Alarms:
- Find alarms with flashing lights and smoke alarms with a strobe light outside the house can catch the attention of neighbors.
- When people who are deaf are asleep, a pillow or bed shaker can wake them so they can escape. The sound of the smoke alarm activates the shaker.
- When people who are hard-of-hearing are asleep, an alert device that uses a loud, mixed, low-pitched sound can wake them.

Low-vision and Blind Accessible: smoke alarms with a vibrating pad are available.

#### What is the leading cause of fires that kill elders, and how can I avoid it?

Smoking is the number one cause of fires that kill elders.
- Never smoke in bed.
- Never smoke if there is an oxygen tank nearby.
- Make sure to use deep and heavy ashtrays to avoid them from flipping or falling off a table by accident.
- When putting out your cigarette, use water or sand to help snuff out any embers.

#### What safe heating habits help prevent burns and fires in older adults' homes?

- Prevent fires and burns by being watchful and alert when you cook.
- Keep children, pets, and things that can burn at least three feet away from radiators, space heaters, fireplaces, wood stoves and furnaces.
- To prevent scalds, set the temperature of your water heater no higher than 120 F (49 C).
- Ask a licensed professional to inspect your electrical and heating system every year, especially if you experience frequently blown fuses or tripped circuit breakers.
- Install carbon monoxide alarms, especially if your home is heated by any source other than electricity.

#### What smoke alarms work best for people in the home with hearing loss?

If someone in your home has hearing loss, consider getting a smoke alarm with low-frequency sounds in the alarm tone.

If anyone in your home is deaf, install a smoke alarm that uses a flashing light or vibration to let you know there is a fire. You can also buy a pillow or bed shaker that will turn on when the smoke alarm sounds.

#### What should I do in the first day after a fire?

1 Day After A Fire Emergency:
- Let family and friends know that you are safe.
- Stay out of fire-damaged homes until a professional says they are OK to re-enter.
- Have injuries checked out by a medical professional.
- Watch out for inhalation injuries and seek medical attention if you get short of breath.
- Wash small wounds with soap and water. Prevent infections by using bandages and replacing them regularly.

#### What should I do in the week after a fire?

1 Week After a Fire Emergency:
- Contact insurance agencies as soon as you can report the when, why, and how the damage occurred.
- Keep receipts for all additional expenses that may occur including lodging, food, or other supplies.
- Prepare a list of damaged home items and keep photographs of all damages.
- Throw away food, beverages, and/or medicine that was exposed to fire, smoke, or soot.
- Check floors and ceiling for signs of sagging.
- Stay connected to your support systems and reach out for help in the following weeks.

#### How do I cope with my mental health after a fire?

It is common for people to experience several stages of adjustment including shock, anger, depression and hopelessness.

Some self-care strategies you may want to consider are:
- Practice stress-reduction techniques such as regular exercise, meditation and deep breathing.
- Allow yourself to feel bad, cry and release negative emotions in a healthy manner.
- Make small decisions daily in order to feel in control of your life.
- Talk about your ordeal with friends and family.
- Focus on what you are thankful for in spite of your loss.
- Get plenty of rest when possible and maintain a normal sleep/wake cycle.

To reach out for free 24/7 counseling or support, call or text the Disaster Distress Helpline at 1-800-985-5990.

#### How do I clean soot and smoke off walls, clothes, and surfaces after a fire?

- Wear rubber gloves and protective clothing.
- Smoke odor and soot can sometimes be washed from clothing that can be bleached. Also, consider washing clothes in cold water with your usual household laundry detergent, and adding one tablespoon of pure vanilla extract.
- To remove soot and smoke from walls, furniture and floors, use a mild soap or detergent or mix together chlorine bleach to every gallon of warm water.
- Be sure to rinse surfaces with clear warm water and dry thoroughly.
- Wash walls one small area at a time, working from the floor up to prevent streaking. Rinse with clear water immediately. Ceilings should be washed last.
- Do not repaint until walls and ceilings are completely dry.
- Reduce the chances of growth of mold and mildew by wiping down all surfaces with a solution of one cup of liquid household bleach to a gallon of water.
- Washable wallpaper can be cleansed like painted walls, but do not wet through the paper.
- Consult a professional about replacing drywall and insulation that has been soaked by water from fire hoses.
- Pots, pans, and flatware should be washed with soapy water, rinsed and then polished.
- Wet debris down to minimize breathing dust particles.

#### What behaviors might kids show after a fire emergency?

Behaviors to look for in kids after a fire emergency:
- Increased anxiety about loved ones
- Anxiety around fire
- Separation anxiety and irritation
- Temper tantrums
- Withdrawal
- Headaches and stomach aches
- Lower school grades
- Sadness

Some children react right away, while others may show signs of difficulty much later. How a child reacts and the common signs of distress can vary according to the child's age, previous experiences, and how the child typically copes with stress. Kids often experience anxiety, nightmares and have difficulty sleeping after an emergency.

#### How can I help my child cope emotionally after a fire?

A child's coping ability is influenced by how their parents and caregivers deal with the crisis. Children will look to adults for guidance, support, and information.

- Talk to kids and help them work through the fear and anxiety they feel after a fire emergency. Try to keep them with you as long as possible, because it helps decrease their anxiety.
- Explain your actions as you work to get everything back in order.
- Get them to talk to you or a healthcare professional, so they get their fears out in the open rather than bottled up inside.
- Help your children feel a sense of control and manage their feelings by encouraging them to take action directly related to the disaster. For example, children can help others after a disaster, including volunteering to help the community or family members in a safe environment.

DO NOT allow children to participate in disaster cleanup activities for health and safety reasons.

#### What should I do for my pet right after escaping a fire?

As soon as you and the animal are a safe distance away from the fire:

- If the animal is coughing or has a runny nose or eyes, ask firefighters to give oxygen to your pet. If the fire department is not there, take your pet to or call the nearest veterinarian for help as soon as you can.
- If your pet has a serious burn (skin has a large or deep open wound), take them to or call the nearest veterinarian as soon as possible.
- Care for any burn injuries and follow any veterinarian instructions given to you.

#### How can I help my pet recover behaviorally after a fire?

Animals may act differently after a traumatic event:
- A scared pet may react by biting or scratching.
- Handle animals carefully and calmly.
- Pets can become upset and react in unusual ways, such as spraying urine, defecating on floors or scratching/biting furnishings.
- Use caution when working with livestock after a fire. Their survival instincts can make normal handling techniques ineffective.

Helping your animal companion heal:
- Care for any burn injuries and follow any veterinarian instructions given to you.
- Use toys, a blanket, or a favorite human's unsoiled clothing to comfort pets.
- Make sure pets are fed their usual diet, and have plenty of water.
- Speak calmly and take some time out to play with them. Doing so can help you in your recovery as well.

#### What signs of distress do elders show after a fire, and how can I support them?

After a traumatic event like a fire, elders will often take longer to recover. Some of the most common signs that caretakers need to be aware of in elders after a fire include:
- Confusion
- Disorientation
- Fear
- Withdrawal
- Anger
- Grief

It is important to surround elders with a strong support network and help them return to their normal routines. Be there for them to talk about the experience. The more they work through their trauma, the easier it will be overall.

#### What protective gear and steps should elders take when returning to a fire-damaged home?

- Discard any food that has been exposed to heat, smoke or soot.
- Stay out of fire-damaged homes until local fire authorities say it is safe to re-enter.
- Wear protective clothing on any exposed skin, including helmets, face masks, gloves, and boots.
- If there is no structural damage to the home, you may still want to wear sturdy footwear and a face mask to protect from stepping on debris or inhaling particulate matter.
- Install new smoke alarms in the home and keep them in good shape.
- Document damages during the fire and take photos.
- There are government assistance programs available for people who have been severely displaced due to a disaster. For less extreme damage, your homeowner's insurance may be able to help with the losses.
